newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols steady, exotics rattle dlr/yen.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols steady, exotics rattle dlr/yen.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options were mostly steady in the U.S., although activity linked to expiration of big exotic options caused turbulence in spot dollar/yen, dealers and analysts said.

"Traders have been generally bullish (on the dollar) and they're trying to stick to that," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc. "But you're starting to see disappointment setting in here."
"In dollar/yen, there's still a lot of people looking for one more spike up," he added. "But it seems the upticks are becoming less frequent and less sustained."
Traders said volatilities, led by the front end, would likely erode if Friday's April U.S. employment report did not lead to a significant move in the dollar.
One-month dollar/yen implied volatility stood at 8.5/8.7 percent, up marginally from late Wednesday levels.
"Implied prices in the middle of the curve are trading at pretty substantial discount to where actual volatilities have been," Revercomb noted.
Three- and six-months were at 8.7/8.8 and 9.1/9.2 percent respectively, a touch firmer on the day.
"There were good offers in this part of the curve even when other maturities were bid up," a Japanese bank trader said.

He said that could be due to vega supply stemming from foreign bond funds that some Japanese securities firms were marketing in Japan. The funds use exotic dollar/yen options to reduce currency risk at low cost for Japanese investors.

Traders said the market did not appear too impressed with the dollar's fresh 4-1/2 year high of 127.47 yen touched overnight because the greenback's rally was partly driven by exotic options and soon fizzled out.
Many traders also attributed the dollar's sudden drop in mid-morning U.S. to selling by an Asian entity that was an original party to the widely talked about reverse knockouts.

According to some bank traders, part of the exotic options expired in Tokyo time without hitting the barrier price around 127.30 yen. The remainder, expiring in New York time at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT were wiped out by the dollar's early rally.
The portion that matured in Tokyo, worth some $800 million, was thus exercised as a deep-in-the-money contract, and the Asian entity sold dollars to square up, traders said.

The New York portion was the result of risk-spreading among banks that had traded the same product with the original market maker, traders said. They added that hedging attempts by the banks at the end of the chain had also affected spot and the short-dated volatilities in recent days.
Dollar/mark volatilities were little changed, with spot hovering at familiar levels ahead of Friday's jobs data. One-month was pegged at 8.4/8.6 percent and one-year at 9.0/9.1, virtually flat.
Short-dated sterling firmed on concerns over the U.K. elections. One-week cable rose 0.5 point to 8.0/9.0 percent.
